notes.b: Businesses chase profit, and that aim can clash with the interests of stakeholders (the people affected by a firm, such as shareholders, employees, customers, creditors and the community). Regulation is the set of rules, set by the State or an independent body, that controls how businesses operate, so that profit-seeking does not come at everyone else's expense.
points: Regulation protects stakeholders such as customers, employees and the public from harm, for example from unsafe products or misleading advertising.
It promotes fair competition, so that no firm gains an advantage by breaking the rules, by colluding with rivals (secretly agreeing with them) or by abusing a dominant position.
It protects safety at work and in the environment, by setting minimum standards that businesses must meet regardless of their profit motive.
It builds trust in markets, which encourages customers, employees and investors to take part, for example by keeping customer deposits in banks secure so that people are willing to save with them.
notes.tip: If asked to outline the purpose of regulation, give the main points in a few words each: protect stakeholders, fair competition, safety and trust. A common mistake is writing a long explanation of just one point.

notes.h: Internal regulation: controls a business sets itself
notes.b: Internal regulation is the set of controls a business puts in place itself, beyond what the law requires. These controls let the firm catch problems early and show stakeholders that it takes its duties seriously.
points: The board of directors (the people elected by shareholders to direct the company) has a legal duty to act in the best interests of the company, to act with care and skill, and to avoid conflicts of interest.

Internal audit is an independent review, carried out inside the firm, of whether controls are working, and it reports its findings to the audit committee or board rather than to the managers whose work it checks.

Risk management means identifying, assessing and controlling events that could stop the business meeting its objectives, such as fraud, a cyber attack or a supply disruption, usually recorded in a risk register.
A compliance function checks that the business obeys laws, regulations and its own policies, and it reports any breaches to senior management so they can be corrected.
A code of conduct sets out expected ethical behaviour for employees and directors, and protected reporting channels let staff raise concerns about wrongdoing without fear of punishment.
notes.tip: When asked how a firm is regulated internally, name the control (internal audit, risk management, compliance function or code of conduct), say what it does and give the reason it protects stakeholders. A common mistake is mixing up internal and external regulation, or naming a control with no explanation.

notes.h: External regulation: law, regulators and auditors
notes.b: External regulation is imposed on a business from outside, by law, by independent statutory bodies (bodies set up by an Act of the Oireachtas, Ireland's parliament) and by independent auditors. A firm has no choice about obeying it.
points: A statutory external audit is required by the Companies Act 2014 for many companies. An audit is an independent check of accounts, and here the independent auditor reports to shareholders on whether the accounts give a true and fair view.

The Central Bank of Ireland regulates and supervises banks, insurers, investment firms and credit unions. It has an enforcement process with sanctions such as fines and reprimands, so it can investigate and penalise firms that breach its rules.
The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) enforces competition and consumer protection law and reviews proposed mergers that could reduce competition.

The Corporate Enforcement Authority, created in 2022, enforces company law. It encourages compliance, investigates companies and directors, can prosecute summarily and can seek the disqualification of a director.
Revenue enforces tax law, the Health and Safety Authority enforces workplace safety, and the Environmental Protection Agency enforces environmental law.
The Data Protection Commission is Ireland's independent data protection authority. It enforces the GDPR, the EU rules on how personal data is collected, stored and used.
notes.tip: A statutory external audit is not the same as internal audit. When naming a regulator, add what it enforces and why that protects stakeholders; a common mistake is naming a regulator with no explanation.

notes.b: Both kinds of regulation protect stakeholders, but they differ in who sets the rules, who checks them and what happens when they are broken. Comparing them side by side keeps them from being confused.
points: Who sets it: internal regulation is set by the business itself, through its board, policies and code of conduct. External regulation is set by law and by statutory bodies, so the firm cannot choose its own standard.

Who enforces it: internal audit, the compliance function and managers check internal rules and report to the board or audit committee. External rules are enforced by independent regulators and by an external auditor who reports to shareholders.

What a breach costs: breaking an internal rule leads to discipline, correction or loss of trust. Breaking external rules can bring fines, prosecution, disqualification of a director and damage to reputation.

Regulation (rules imposed by law or a regulator), governance (how a company directs and controls itself) and compliance (obeying the rules) are different things. Governance is wider than compliance, because it also covers culture and decision-making.
notes.tip: Keep internal audit (inside the firm, reporting to the board or audit committee) separate from statutory external audit (an independent auditor reporting to shareholders on the accounts).

notes.b: In a company the owners (shareholders) are separate from the people who run it, so there must be a system that keeps those in charge answerable. Corporate governance is the system of rules, practices and processes by which a company is directed and controlled.
points: Accountability means directors answer to shareholders and other stakeholders for their decisions and results, and transparency means disclosing accurate information on time so that stakeholders can judge those results.
A board usually combines executive directors, who run the business day to day, with non-executive directors, who are independent of daily management and bring independent scrutiny to decisions.
Good governance often separates the roles of chair (who leads the board) and chief executive (who leads the management), so that no single person holds unchecked power over the business.
Board committees do specialist work: an audit committee oversees financial reporting and internal audit, and a remuneration committee sets executive pay.
Shareholders exercise governance rights by voting at the annual general meeting, including on the appointment and removal of directors.
Strong governance is a form of ethics in practice, because it sets the culture that decides whether controls are respected or ignored.
notes.tip: To explain governance, define it, then give accountability and transparency with an effect, for example separate chair and chief executive roles prevent unchecked power. A common mistake is confusing governance with management.

notes.b: The specification's glossary defines it this way: "ESG stands for environmental, social and governance and These factors form the pillars in ESG frameworks and businesses may in some cases be expected to report their performance and progress under these three pillars." Investors and other stakeholders use the three pillars to judge a company's sustainability and ethics.
points: Environmental factors cover carbon emissions, energy use, water use, waste and pollution, for example a food company cutting the packaging waste it sends to landfill.
Social factors cover employees' health and safety, pay and diversity, fair treatment of customers and suppliers, and the effect of the business on its local community.

Governance factors cover board structure, executive pay, anti-bribery controls, tax transparency and the protection of shareholder rights. This is the 'G' in ESG, the factors a company reports on, whereas corporate governance is the system itself.
Environmental and social harm can cost a business customers, staff and access to finance, so managing ESG risk is a practical form of business sustainability.
Greenwashing, which means claiming better environmental performance than the evidence supports, is the ethical failure of ESG reporting, because it misleads the stakeholders who rely on the report.
notes.tip: If asked to identify the three elements of an ESG report, write three short labels: environmental, social, governance, and add one example of each. A common mistake is writing 'economic' or 'sustainable' as the third factor, or writing 'governance' with no meaning.

notes.b: An ESG report discloses how a company performs on environmental, social and governance factors, usually alongside its financial results. Firms report because stakeholders now expect it, and in some cases the law requires it.
points: Investors and lenders use ESG reports to judge long-term risks, such as climate-related disruption or abuse in the supply chain, which can affect future profits.
Reporting builds stakeholder trust and can help a business win contracts from customers that set sustainability standards for their suppliers.

The EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD, an EU law that member states must write into their own law) requires the companies it covers to publish standardised sustainability reports under the European Sustainability Reporting Standards, within the directors' report.
Ireland transposed the CSRD into Irish law on 5 July 2024, by S.I. No. 336 of 2024 (European Union (Corporate Sustainability Reporting) Regulations 2024), amended by S.I. No. 498 of 2024.

Scope and dates have changed since 2024. A 2025 EU directive delayed the later reporting waves by two years, and Ireland gave it effect in July 2025 by S.I. No. 309 of 2025. The EU then narrowed the scope of the CSRD in 2026, so fewer companies must report.
Assurance (an independent check of the report) is a requirement of the Directive's reporting regime, so the information is not left entirely to the company's own judgement.
Digital tools support this, because electronic reporting and digital audit trails make ESG and financial data easier to record, check and publish.
notes.tip: If asked why a business reports on ESG, link a reason (investors judge long-term risk, trust, winning contracts) to its effect on a named stakeholder. A common mistake is describing the pillars without saying why reporting matters.

notes.b: Regulation and governance bring benefits and costs, and how well they work depends on how consistently they are applied. An evaluation weighs both sides and reaches a justified conclusion.
points: The benefits are protection for stakeholders, greater trust and a level playing field between firms that obey the rules.
The costs are compliance expenses and staff time, which weigh more heavily on small and medium enterprises, because they have few staff to handle reporting.
Over-regulation can slow innovation and deter entrepreneurs, while under-regulation allows fraud, unsafe practices and environmental damage to go unchecked.
Regulation works best when it is enforced consistently and when businesses adopt internal controls that go beyond the legal minimum.
notes.tip: When asked to evaluate regulation, give a benefit and a cost, for example the cost on small firms, and finish with a justified conclusion. A common mistake is a one-sided answer.

notes.h: Irish news examples: Coinbase Ireland, PTSB and the HSE
notes.b: Applying the ideas to real events shows how regulation, internal controls and ownership affect stakeholders. Each example below names the rule or control involved and one effect.
points: In October 2026 the Central Bank of Ireland announced a fine of €3,252,618 on Coinbase Ireland Limited (a 30% settlement discount from €4,646,597). The sanction was subject to High Court confirmation.
The breaches were of safeguarding and outsourcing obligations under the Electronic Money Regulations 2011, between 1 November 2020 and 19 August 2025.

The Central Bank's findings were inadequate outsourcing governance, customer funds not adequately safeguarded, and weak internal controls and escalation. This shows external regulation, internal controls and governance, and the risk to customers' money damages trust in markets.
Earlier, Coinbase Europe was fined about €21.5m for anti-money-laundering failures in late 2025, confirmed by the High Court in January 2026.
In April 2026 PTSB agreed to be sold to BAWAG for about €1.6 billion; the State held about 57% after the post-crisis bailout. PTSB shareholders approved the offer on 30 July 2026.
Approvals from the High Court and the ECB were still needed, with completion expected in late 2026 or early 2027. This shows a change of ownership (privatisation) that still depends on regulation.

The Data Protection Commission fined the HSE €645,000 over its handling of paper health records at former hospital sites in Mullingar and Letterkenny. The final decision was dated 28 August 2026 and announced on 2 September 2026.
The fine was for an infringement of the GDPR storage limitation principle, and it shows a public body being held accountable for how it handles personal data.
notes.tip: In a news-based question, use the facts in the stimulus to name the rule or control involved and its effect on stakeholders. A common mistake is making general comments about regulation with no link to the case.

questions.prompt: Explain how corporate governance, internal controls and external regulation work together to protect stakeholders, and evaluate the effectiveness of each.
questions.model: Corporate governance sets the framework of accountability and transparency, so the board answers to shareholders for its decisions and the company discloses accurate information. Internal controls such as risk management, internal audit and a compliance function detect and prevent problems before they harm stakeholders, for example by stopping fraud in payment processes. External regulation sets minimum standards that every firm must meet, such as the statutory audit under the Companies Act 2014, and it gives regulators such as the Central Bank powers to investigate and penalise. Evaluation: internal controls are flexible and suited to the business, but they can be weakened by a board that ignores them, while external regulation is independent but can be backward-looking and costly for smaller firms. Protection is strongest when all three operate together, because governance sets the culture, internal controls catch problems early and regulation provides a safety net.

questions.prompt: Explain the three elements of an ESG report and why investors and lenders value it.
questions.model: Environmental factors, such as carbon emissions and resource use, show the company's impact on the planet and its exposure to climate risk. Social factors, such as employee welfare, diversity and supply chain practices, show how the company treats people. Governance factors, such as board structure and executive pay, show how well the company is directed and controlled. Investors and lenders value this information because non-financial risks can damage future profits, and reporting lets them compare firms and judge long-term sustainability.
